messenger_reliability.builder_why: Two of the three blocking findings against this row are closed on the glass, and the third — the scroll — is not, and I am withdrawing what I said about it. A message the far phone refuses can be sent again: `send it again` clears the refusal and kicks the round, and reliability.json's eighteenth and nineteenth capabilities walk it end to end (refusal_and_retry, pairing_refused). But I looked at 13 before writing this and the way out is not on the picture: the row reads 'it would not go ✕' and the retry lives in the long-press menu, which is where the reader was told last cycle there was nothing. A dead end whose exit is behind a gesture with no hint is still a dead end, and the next version puts the words in the margin beside the refusal where the timestamp is. A message arriving at a shut phone is a picture now rather than an empty window: logs/reception.json records permission granted, six arrivals at the service worker and six banners drawn, one still held by the browser, each with its kind, who it was from and how loud it was allowed to be. It had failed for a reason worth writing down — the record asked for a silent notification and a vibration in the same call, which Chromium refuses outright, so the phone was told and could not draw it. 13 is the artifact this row is named for and it carries what it waited for: partner_typing true, read at the shutter by the same function the glass asks; four delivery states in the picture's own words (read, sent, sent, 'it would not go'); a reaction, an edit, a take-back and three read markers folded in and named. 12 asks a word the pictures answer — query 'morning', six hits, the type filter on photographs, kinds {photo: 6}. Every seeded scene is paired and connected against a far phone carrying the same year, 14,062 to 14,113 events each, and 08's own sync numbers are in its record: 388 rounds, 8 pushed, 9 pulled, no faults. And for the first time all five clips pass their own check on this capture's frames — 310, 421, 300, 376 and 518 frames, none of them held, none of them a jump in the light. What I claimed and withdraw: a commit of mine four hours ago says the scroll's build spikes are closed — '1 of 621 frames over 400 ms, build p95 24 ms'. The capture measured the same build on the same machine and says otherwise. logs/scroll_webkit.json: 203 of 793 frames over 400 ms, build p95 897, max 1676, against the previous capture's 189 of 789 at p95 688 — no improvement, slightly worse. The distribution is bimodal, 6 ms or about 775 with nothing between, one spike every three to five frames, which is the rate at which a fling at 3000 px/s brings a new note into a 780 pt viewport. The probe that said 24 ms measured something this capture does not do, and the capture is the evidence. What I can say about the cause is a reading of the code rather than a fourth guess: handwriting goes through Inked, which is a ShaderMask, so every note's subtree needs a compositing layer, so its tear cannot be drawn straight into the canvas and has to be composed as an image by SlicedMasks.at — and that key is tear@WxH with one tear per note out of a pool of 56, so the height bucket that was meant to let four notes in five find one already made saves nothing. The next thing I do is put SlicedMasks.composed into the capture's own record and re-shoot the one scene, so the number comes from the artifact and not from me. Also still against this row: no second device anywhere in the set; transport local on every reliability run, with the tailnet recorded pending for want of a key this session may not ask for again; a first launch that imports the year still costs seconds; and one console error in the whole capture, a 401 during 14, whose request the harness does not name.

material_truth.builder_why: The pale one-pixel rule is still gone, and this time on ten stills every one of which was taken by this capture rather than on a set half of which predated it: tools/check/hairline.py reads zero bright one-row runs of 60 px or more on the wood in all ten. Eight notes on 02 sit on eight different torn edges with no repeat. What has not moved is the two things this row was actually held down by. Repeated letters: 513 marks of ink on the thread still, laid over each other, median best-fit IoU 0.669, and the share with a near twin is 0.166 at 0.80, 0.058 at 0.85, 0.012 at 0.90 and 0.000 at 0.99 — no letter is drawn exactly twice, but one mark in six has a twin close enough to see. And the desk: nothing was done to the wood this cycle, so a reading that its grain has almost no structure across the grain stands as measured. What did change is small and real: the margin row no longer wears an Opacity over the ink — the caret and the delivery mark are drawn in paler ink instead, which is both the honest way to draw a faint pen and one less compositing layer over a piece of paper. Still true and still against this row: paper is packed as WebP at Blender's default quality, so every number here is measured against an already-degraded ceiling, and I have never compared any of it with a photograph of real paper. And the same flat slab the anti-goal row loses points for is this row's too: on 07 at frame 380 an authored feeling lands on a pale square card whose luma standard deviation is 0.87 over 80 px, against 4.58 for the flattest patch of real paper anywhere on 02_chat and 33.6 for the median. The cause is in the object renders rather than in the app: 80 px windows inside obj_dog_ear's own packed surface have a median local standard deviation of 0.89, against 9.0 to 9.6 for the paper stocks. Eight objects are paper and none of them has any tooth. And it is not the WebP pass either, which was the next thing I would have blamed: the 1200 px source render of obj_dog_ear reads a median local standard deviation of 0.97 over the same window, against 0.89 for the packed one. The surface was never there. Nor is it one object: sampling eight frames across 08, every one of them has a pale 80 px patch flatter than 2.5 and most are under 1.6, against 4.58 for the flattest pale patch of real paper anywhere on a full screen of it. I have not gone through them one at a time — the check does that, and writing the check is the first thing the next cycle does.

emotional_transmission.builder_why: The one scene that shows a state change reaching a shut phone is a picture now instead of a blank window on a black desktop, and the record says what the page asked for and what the worker drew. 07 is 421 frames with none held and no jump in the light; the hole at frame 220 that failed the ninth capture is 5.6 grey levels at a declared cut now, against 22.9, and it closed because the run waits for the paper to arrive — MaskCache's own count of what is still decoding — rather than for a number somebody guessed at. The viewer keeps the corner that reaches a feeling and the ambient strip above it, so opening a photograph no longer costs the emotional layer. 08 and 15 are this capture's rather than the last one's, which is the difference between evidence and a copy on disk. What stands, and it is the whole of what holds this row back: no artifact in this set was made by a device that can vibrate — channel_here is 'page' for every capture — so the row's own test, a feeling identifiable by its pattern with the screen face down, cannot be run on anything here; and there is no frame anywhere of a gesture on one device becoming a sensation on the other.

coherence.builder_why: The records agree with each other in places where they did not. spine/types.dart and docs/EVENT_TYPES.md name the same eighteen types, and a test fails on the next drift. A length reads the same way wherever it is written: clockOf gives 0:07 in the gallery and in the viewer, where the gallery used to say 2s beside a voice note saying 0:52; dayLabel takes a String, an int or a DateTime and says the same day for all three. A phone that is not paired any more says so on the card as well as in the log, instead of carrying the partner's standing line above 'not paired yet'. The thread's own record names every kind it folded in — reactions, edits, deletions, read markers — rather than only the rows it drew, and DIFF.json says what happened to each artifact rather than only how far it moved. Two tests that certified nothing certify something now: the module-cost test no longer passes on a bare substring of a 256-word pairing vocabulary, and the row-height probe has assertions instead of a debugPrint. What is still open and I have not touched it: the same thread row is drawn two ways inside one evidence set, in 07 and in 08. And the code half of this row still carries what I think is the most serious thing in the repository — nothing in capture.sh, run.sh or bootstrap.sh ever runs flutter test, so every structural guarantee this row rests on is held by a suite that no script has to pass before an artifact is taken. One more I found by looking at the frames myself. The haptic lane, which 07 is required to carry, sits at the top edge 'where the app draws only desk' — except in Chat, where the top edge is the ambient strip, so its blocks and its red playhead lie across the partner's standing line. The comment above it records the same fault being fixed once already, on the composer. An annotation on a recording is a ruler laid beside the thing; the next version of it is drawn into the clip under the frame, not into the app.

anti_goal.builder_why: Both findings from the last review are closed, and then I found a third one myself, which is why this is not the ten I was going to write. The heart was the last symbol in the drawer — obj_heart_fold, item 27 of the 30 the authoring sheet offers — and it is gone, so nothing in the object set is a picture of a feeling rather than a thing that could be on a desk. The manifest no longer lists fourteen of fifteen artifacts as older than the capture that claims them: this run wrote every one of them, and every check written beside them now says which run wrote it, because a verdict left over from the previous capture reads exactly like a fresh one and I believed one for an hour today. There are no badges, no points, no streak warnings and no guilt in any string; tools/lint/strings.py reads every display literal and passes; the app never names itself and never addresses a user. Claiming a whole row is a strong claim, so here is what takes it back: whether a surface reads as an approximation of paper rather than as a photograph of one is this row's to fail as much as the material row's, and I cannot judge that from inside. If a reader sees the desk as a procedural texture, this is a 7 and not a 10. And one thing I found in this capture's own clip that this row cannot survive intact: an authored feeling lands on a flat slab. 07, the last run, frames 314 to about 400, on the Us page — the object arrives on a pale, square-cornered, untextured card with a drop shadow under it. Measured on frame 380: two 80 px patches of that card read a standard deviation of 0.87 and 1.00 in luma, against 32.5 and 43.2 on the module strips either side of it in the same frame, and against 4.58 for the flattest pale 80 px patch of real paper anywhere on 02_chat (median 33.6 over 288 of them). It is five times flatter than the flattest paper in the set. That is the brief's own sentence: a beige rectangle with a drop shadow is a failure of the whole visual concept, and it is drawn here for about a second and a half in a clip every reader watches. I thought at first it was a piece drawing before its paper arrived, and it is not: I measured the objects themselves. Inside the packed renders, 80 px windows of an object's own surface have a median local standard deviation of 0.89 on obj_dog_ear, 1.08 on obj_bookmark, 1.36 on obj_torn_corner and 2.49 on obj_ticket, against 9.0 to 9.6 for the paper stocks measured the same way. The paper-shaped feeling objects are rendered with a smooth surface and no tooth at all, so a card lying on the desk is a shaded fill with a shadow under it. It is the folds' fault from cycle three, in the objects this time: the material is right and the surface is not in it. The same card is on 11 at frame 0 (0.74) and the same slab lands in 15. The fix is in blender/objects/objects.py, and the check that would have caught it reads the glass rather than the assets — no pale rectangle on screen may be flatter than the flattest real paper. And it is not the WebP pass either, which was the next thing I would have blamed: the 1200 px source render of obj_dog_ear reads a median local standard deviation of 0.97 over the same window, against 0.89 for the packed one. The surface was never there. Nor is it one object: sampling eight frames across 08, every one of them has a pale 80 px patch flatter than 2.5 and most are under 1.6, against 4.58 for the flattest pale patch of real paper anywhere on a full screen of it. I have not gone through them one at a time — the check does that, and writing the check is the first thing the next cycle does.
